annotations.annotation_text: Page 392 opens Book 2, Chapter 4 ("Tristan and Isolde") during the Age of Heroes (closing) phase. This passage continues the voyage of Tristan and Isolde observed by the Four Old Men as seagulls, Wagnerian chromatic motifs, King Mark's displacement, featuring Tristan, Isolde, Mamalujo, King Mark. The nocturnal dream-narrative layers Dublin topography, world mythology, and linguistic alchemy into polysemic prose.

annotations.annotation_text: Mid-page polysemic node on page 392 ("Tristan and Isolde"): Joyce weaves multilingual puns across 60+ languages — etymological roots from the Contemporary Literature Press lexicons (Romanian, Scandinavian, Slavic, Classical) intersect with local Dublin speech rhythms. The Age of Heroes (closing) dream-logic transforms ordinary syntax into a palimpsest of global literary and mythic references.
sources: Tindall, William York. A Reader's Guide to Finnegans Wake. https://archive.org/details/readersguidetofi00tind
Contemporary Literature Press: Multilingual Lexicons for FW. https://editura.mttlc.ro
Atherton, James S. The Books at the Wake. https://archive.org/details/booksatwake0000athe

annotations.annotation_text: Fall/resurrection motif "wall" on page 392 ("Tristan and Isolde"): Tim Finnegan tumbling from his ladder, Humpty Dumpty shattering from the wall, Adam falling in Eden — all converge within the voyage of Tristan and Isolde observed by the Four Old Men as seagulls, Wagnerian chromatic motifs, King Mark's displacement. The comic-cosmic Fall during the Age of Heroes (closing) phase demands its counterpart: resurrection through the whiskey-splash of the water of life (uisce beatha).
sources: The Ballad of Tim Finnegan's Wake. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finnegan%27s_Wake
